analysis.one_liner: Limits injury lawsuits against contractors on federally funded construction projects when the worker was partly at fault.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its September 2020 referral to the House Judiciary Committee, receiving no hearing or vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar 'absolute liability' — strict legal responsibility regardless of anyone's own carelessness — for falls and other gravity-related injuries on infrastructure projects that use federal money, covering the owners and contractors on those projects. Instead, states would have to apply a comparative-negligence standard, meaning an injured worker's own carelessness would reduce or erase recovery. That would override strict-liability rules like New York's Scaffold Law, which makes contractors responsible for fall hazards on elevation work, for any project touched by federal funding.
analysis.who_benefits: Property owners, contractors, and their liability insurers on federally funded construction projects. They gain protection from lawsuits holding them fully responsible for fall and gravity-related injuries even when their own safety failures caused them, which would lower their legal exposure and insurance costs. The largest real-world effect would fall on New York, whose Scaffold Law imposes strict liability on contractors for elevation injuries, and the bill's sponsor and cosponsor both represented New York districts [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits lawsuits on an absolute-liability basis against property owners or contractors for injuries tied to elevation or gravity-related risks on federally owned or federally funded infrastructure projects [S2] [S3].

It requires states to apply a comparative-negligence standard that considers the injured person's own carelessness — such as not following safety training, not using provided safety equipment, or being impaired — when that negligence helped cause the injury [S2] [S3].

For the contractors and property owners affected, that reduces liability exposure: recovery for an injured worker would be reduced or eliminated in proportion to the worker's own fault, even if the contractor's safety failures also caused the fall [S3].

The bill does not preempt state workers' compensation laws, so injured workers would still receive workers' comp benefits — but workers' comp replaces only a fraction of full damages available in a lawsuit [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Injured construction workers on federally funded projects. A worker hurt in a fall who was partly careless — for example, briefly not clipping a harness — could see recovery cut proportionally or barred entirely, even where the contractor also failed to provide required fall protection. The difference would shift onto workers' families, and to public programs when workers' compensation falls short.
analysis.who_pays_short: Injured construction workers and their families

drawbacks.text: Falls are a leading cause of death on construction sites, and strict liability for elevation work is the mechanism that pushes property owners and contractors to provide and maintain fall protection; replacing it with comparative fault weakens that safety pressure and shifts part of the cost of an injury onto the person who was hurt [S2] [S3].

The bill reaches any project 'directly or indirectly' using federal financial assistance, which covers an enormous share of highways, bridges, transit, and public buildings, so the liability shield would apply far beyond the narrow set of projects its sponsor highlighted [S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge the real cost side: absolute liability can hold a party responsible for an injury even when the injured worker ignored safety training and equipment, and the resulting exposure raises insurance premiums that flow into project bids on public infrastructure [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The savings to contractors and their insurers are real but modest relative to the loss on the worker side: strict liability for elevation work is a deliberate safety-forcing rule, and diluting it on federally funded projects trades away the strongest legal incentive for fall protection in exchange for lower insurance costs. The bill offered nothing in return for injured workers beyond existing workers' compensation.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced in September 2020, and the committee never scheduled a hearing or vote, so the bill died there when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Chris Jacobs introduced the bill on September 11, 2020, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S1] [S5].

No further action was ever taken: the action history shows only introduction and the committee referral, with no hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].
The bill drew one cosponsor, Rep. Tom Reed, also of New York [S3] [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never became law, construction contractors and their insurers on federally funded projects gained nothing, and injured workers kept whatever strict-liability remedies their state law provides, including New York's Scaffold Law. The outcome leaves the existing legal framework — and the workers it protects — in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Injured workers, since the liability shield died in committee

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were New York Republicans, but no hearing or vote was ever held, so the record shows no partisan pattern of support or opposition.

industries.note: The bill would shield them from full legal responsibility for gravity-related injuries on federally funded projects whenever the injured worker was partly at fault, cutting their lawsuit exposure. That gain comes directly out of injured workers' recoveries and weakens the legal incentive to maintain fall protection.

Lower liability exposure on federal-aid projects would reduce the premiums insurers can charge, and carriers have long pressed for changes like this in New York. Workers would bear the cost through reduced recoveries, while the safety-forcing effect of strict liability — the reason those premiums are high — would be diluted.
